en: The Sūtra on the Fundamental Nature of All Dharmas Spoken by the Buddha, translated from the *Madhyama Āgama* as a separate version by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi during the Wu Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The Buddha...
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen as I explain the root of all dharmas.
They replied:
“Yes, indeed,” [the bhikṣus replied].
The World-Honored One said:
“If there are followers of external paths and heterodox teachings who come to question you:”
"What is called the root of all phenomena?
One should answer:
"Desire is the root of all phenomena."
What is meant by "habituation" (āsevana)?
It is repeated practice.
What is meant by "converging toward the same destination" (ekāyana)?
Suffering is of the same nature [as existence].
What is meant by "leading to existence"?
It is mindfulness that leads to existence.
What is called the path of illumination?
Contemplation is the path of illumination.
What is called the foremost?
Samādhi is foremost.
What is called supreme? Wisdom is supreme.
What is meant by "firm"?
Liberation is firm.
What is meant by "ultimate"?
“Nirvāṇa is the ultimate. “Thus it is, monks! Desire is the root of all phenomena;

desire is further the condition for all phenomena. Feeling is the convergence of all phenomena; mindfulness is what brings all phenomena into existence. Reflection is the illumination of the path for all phenomena; samādhi is the foremost among all phenomena; wisdom is the supreme among all phenomena; liberation is the firmness of all phenomena; and nirvāṇa is the ultimate of all phenomena.”

“Monks! You should train yourselves thus: you should constantly maintain the perception of homelessness; the perception of impermanence; the perception of suffering in what is impermanent; the perception of non-self in what is suffering; the perception of foulness in food; the perception of impurity; the perception of death; the perception that there is no delight in any world; the perception of knowing the wrong and the right regarding the world; and the perception of discerning existence and non-existence within the world.”
One should know, through right view, the pleasures practiced and grasped by the world, their transformation and loss, and their ultimate destination. Monks!
To be mindful of this is to sever craving, abandon desire, enter into right wisdom, and reach the end of suffering.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, they all rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
This is the *Sūtra on the Fundamental Nature of All Dharmas* spoken by the Buddha.
